title: Interest rates: Economists warn rate rises still on horizon
full_text:
Investors may be breathing a sigh of relief after this week's benign inflation report, but a group of economists argues that Australia's central bank will likely lift interest rates one more time this year, given the higher costs related to the conflict in the Middle East.
Brendan Rynne, chief economist at KPMG, warned the economy was still running too hot, unlike Canada and New Zealand where demand was starting to cool. Australia, he said, was not getting a boost from stronger productivity, which meant excess spending would keep driving up prices.
"It's this outlook that suggests that the need for an additional interest rate increase in the near term to dampen demand further is more likely than not," he said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has already lifted the cash rate three times in quick succession this year, which has pushed the cash rate to 4.35 per cent - the highest level in more than two years - to tame resurgent inflation.
While traders have abandoned bets for an imminent rate rise after consumer prices for the June quarter undershot forecasts, they still believe the next move will be higher.
Before the report, markets had implied a one-in-five chance of a rate rise in August. For the rest of the year, traders are pricing in a 50 per cent chance the RBA will lift the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by year-end. The RBA, which holds its next policy meeting on August 11, is expected to maintain its hardline rhetoric on inflation.
"I don't think they're going to drop their concern about inflation just yet," said Citi senior economist Faraz Syed. "I think they'll maintain a fairly hawkish tone, and they'll continue to say that a hold in August does not mean no further rate rises in the future."
Even so, the softer-than-anticipated inflation report prompted Goldman Sachs and Westpac to entirely give up their calls for higher borrowing costs. Just last month, Westpac was tipping two more rate increases by Christmas.
"The material downside surprise relative to expectations shifts the balance of risks towards the RBA remaining on hold for the remainder of 2026," said Andrew Boak, Goldman Sachs' chief economist for Australia, in a note.
Yet, forecasters at Citi, UBS, AMP, Bank of Queensland, Rabobank, Barrenjoey, Deloitte, KPMG and Judo Bank are sticking to the view that the next move in borrowing costs is up, not down.
The RBA led developed economies in being the first to raise interest rates as it struggled to contain runaway prices even before the Iran war sent the oil price soaring above $US100 a barrel.
Core inflation, the central bank's preferred measure because it excludes volatile items, hit 3.6 per cent in the 12 months to June, well above its 2.5 per cent midpoint target.
"Inflation has been above the target band for a material period of time. So they won't be comfortable with it," Syed said.
Making matters worse for policymakers, inflation is likely to re-accelerate.
Citi and Barrenjoey forecast core, or trimmed mean inflation, to climb 1 per cent in the September quarter, faster than the 0.8 per cent recorded in the June quarter.
Such an outcome would be too high for policy makers to ignore.
"We think the RBA will hike in November," Barrenjoey chief economist Jo Masters said.
Complicating the outlook is the re-escalation of the Middle East conflict.
As the US and Iran continue to trade strikes, oil prices have headed back towards $US100 a barrel.
"The unresolved Middle East war potentially puts even more pressures on fuel prices this time around given that the world has been running down reserves, which could translate into more fuel surcharges across services," AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina said.
She believes the risk still tilts toward higher borrowing costs this year, a view that is also shared by Ben Picton, a senior rate strategist at Rabobank.
"We still have a hike pencilled in for November," he said.
"With fuel excise cut rolling off, and higher crude and product prices courtesy of the war restarting, we should see a bit of payback in the months ahead."
The Australian government granted motorists a temporary fuel excise relief to help households cope with a surge in oil prices driven by the war in Iran. But that relief expires on Sunday, just as oil prices climb to nearly $US90, up from $US70 before the war started in late February.
Meanwhile, the US Federal Reserve overnight on Wednesday left its cash rate on hold but new chairman Kevin Warsh failed to convince the market that it was committed to bringing inflation back to target.
As a result bond yields shot up and traders are pricing in a 92 per cent chance of rate rise in the world's largest economy by Christmas.
